findings.issue: Source: "to devise evil for the Trojans"; candidate: "to plan trouble for the Trojans" softens the phrase (p28 renders the same idea as "plotted evil"). Also "exceedingly angry" became "furiously angry", which sharpens it.
findings.fix: Poseidon was exceedingly angry that his grandson Amphimachus had fallen. He went to the tents and ships of the Achaeans to urge the Danaans on still further and to devise evil for the Trojans. Idomeneus met him as he was leaving a comrade who had just come from the fight, wounded in the knee. His fellow soldiers had carried the man off the field. Idomeneus gave orders to the physicians and went on to his tent, for he was still thirsting for battle. Poseidon spoke in the likeness and with the voice of Thoas son of Andraemon, who ruled the Aetolians of all Pleuron and high Calydon and was honored among his people as if he were a god. “Idomeneus,” he said, “lawgiver to the Cretans, what has become of the threats the sons of the Achaeans used to make against the Trojans?”

findings.issue: Source: "Meriones, peer of Mars"; candidate: "the equal of Ares". Elsewhere in this book (p36, p52) "peer of" is kept, so the Butler phrase is rendered inconsistently.
findings.fix: At this, Meriones, peer of Ares, went to the tent and got himself a bronze spear. He followed after Idomeneus, set on great deeds of valor. As when baneful Ares goes out to battle, and his son Panic, strong and dauntless, goes with him to strike terror even into the heart of a hero—the pair have left Thrace to arm themselves among the Ephyri or the brave Phlegyans, but they will not listen to both of the contending armies, and will give victory to one side or the other—so Meriones and Idomeneus, captains of men, went out to battle in their bronze armor. Meriones spoke first. “Son of Deucalion,” he said, “where would you have us begin fighting? On the right wing of the army, in the center, or on the left wing, where I think the Achaeans will be weakest?”

findings.issue: Source: "Meriones, peer of fleet Mars"; candidate: "the equal of swift Ares". Inconsistent with "peer of Ares" used for the same formula in p36 and p52.
findings.fix: Meriones, peer of swift Ares, then led the way until they came to the part of the army that Idomeneus had named.

findings.issue: Butler's garbled "a redoubtable dispenser of death battle" (missing "in"); candidate reads sensibly as "a fearsome dealer of death in battle".

Source "sprang upon him like a vulture, drew the spear from his shoulder" leaves unclear whose shoulder (Ascalaphus's, from Deiphobus's throw); candidate keeps the same ambiguity ("sprang on him ... out of his shoulder"). Acceptable, but could name Ascalaphus.
